items: Understand God. Remember who we are.

In Uday Kumar’s teaching, God is the shared Creator appearing through every life. The game of experiences gives the mind a clear picture of this identity: we designed the game, entered its roles, and became absorbed in them. Remembering the same Creator in ourselves and others brings that understanding into the way we live.

Why this website exists

Confusion about God can leave people vulnerable to fear, division, and manipulation in God’s name. Uday’s purpose is to make the divine identity understandable through a simple philosophical explanation, so recognition can become a state of mind from which we meet the world. A more peaceful world is the hope guiding this work.
Picture the beginning
One Creator. Many lives. A game of experiences.

Imagine being the one Creator, able to create anything, but alone, with nobody else to meet. In Uday’s story, that aloneness becomes boredom. You create a world of relationships, discoveries, joy, and difficulty, and enter it through its many lives. A worker, a parent, a friend, and a stranger are roles in this game. The shared Creator is who we are beneath those roles.

Before entering, we designed how the game would unfold. From inside, we cannot rewrite its complete design. Our choices, work, learning, forgetting, and remembrance are themselves parts of the unfolding. We can fully participate without demanding control over the whole or knowing the next scene.
Follow the complete explanation
Make the divine identity visible in life.

A tree growing, a child learning, a person creating, and someone who disagrees with us can all invite remembrance of the same Creator. Here, making God visible means giving the mind an understandable picture of shared identity and meeting living beings through it. The story is a doorway into that understanding.
A state of mind to live from

We can laugh, grieve, love, work, and help while remembering who we are. The movie shows how a scene absorbs us; the lotus shows remaining within life with inward lightness. Understanding is intended to loosen the grip of a passing role and let care arise through recognition of the same Creator.
Understanding God includes the person before us.

In this teaching, another person’s religion cannot place them outside the shared Creator. Respect includes listening, allowing sincere disagreement, and protecting people from harm. A promise of divine reward cannot make someone’s life disposable. Remembering our common identity gives us a reason to question manipulation rather than turn against an entire community.

An old insight, a simple explanation

The Vedic and Upanishadic pointers to Brahman and the Self, and Ashtavakra’s teachings on awareness and oneness, are close companions to this enquiry. Uday’s Creator-and-game story brings that insight into a scene people can visualize. Study the passages, understand the connection, and let the meaning carry into ordinary life.

This page is part of one enquiry: understand the Creator, remember our shared identity, and participate in life with care.
Understand the teaching: questions and answers

Bring the questions that matter to you: What is God? Who are we? Why did we enter this game? How can remembrance change the way we treat one another? These answers develop Uday’s explanation and welcome sincere questioning.

Begin by understanding the Creator-and-game story. Then return to it in a real scene: a disagreement, a changed plan, or a moment of joy. Remember the same Creator in yourself and the people involved. The examples below help connect understanding with participation; you can explore them at your own pace.

This explanation gives the mind a picture of the divine identity and a way to remember it while life continues. Read the story, explore its scriptural connections, and see how the same Creator includes the person before you.
From understanding God to living together

Uday’s aim is clarity that enters relationships: to understand the Creator, remember who we are during experience, and recognize the same identity in every life. Confusion can be exploited through fear, promises, money, or demands for obedience. This teaching asks us to examine those demands and meet others through shared identity, including people of other religions.
When faith becomes a reason for division
Someone tells you that people of another religion are enemies of God and that harming them will earn a divine reward. The role of loyal follower may feel pressured to obey or afraid to question.

Return to the whole teaching: we are the Creator who designed and entered this game, and cannot rewrite its design from inside. The person being targeted shares the same Creator. Their religion does not remove their life from our shared identity. A promised reward cannot replace that recognition.

Question the claim and its source. Refuse to participate in harm, protect anyone at risk where you safely can, and seek appropriate lawful help. Those responses unfold within the game. Challenge the person or organization promoting violence while recognizing innocent people who share their faith.
Does the belief being presented include the same Creator in the person it asks me to reject? What response protects life and allows honest questioning?
Why is understanding God central to this website?

Uday’s purpose is to make the divine identity clear enough to imagine and remember in everyday life. The Creator-and-game story explains who we are, why we experience different roles, and why the person before us shares the same source. Understanding is intended to become a state of mind expressed through participation, respect, and care.
What does making God visible mean here?

It means helping the mind picture the shared Creator through the game story and recognize that identity in living beings. The website invites you to meet creation with remembrance: the person, tree, relationship, and experience are within the same game. This is a way of understanding God through Uday’s philosophy, rather than a photograph of a separate being.
Does this teaching ask me to leave my religion?

No. Uday offers an explanation to study and enquire into. You can remain within your tradition, compare its teachings, and disagree sincerely. Religions use different accounts of God; respect does not require pretending they all say the same thing. Here, the shared Creator includes people of every faith and people who hold no religious belief.
How can I recognize manipulation in God’s name?

Examine claims that demand unquestioning obedience, money, hostility toward another community, or harm in exchange for divine reward. Ask what the claim says, where it comes from, and what it asks you to do to a living person. In Uday’s teaching, that person shares the same Creator. You can refuse harm, protect others, and question the teacher, including Uday and this website.

In Uday’s story, the one Creator was alone, with the power to create anything but nobody else to meet. That aloneness becomes boredom, and the Creator makes a game of many lives and experiences and enters it. The story gives the mind a picture of our shared identity. Remembering that source while fully experiencing life is the aim of the teaching.

Ashtavakra emphasizes the Self as already free and beyond individual doership. Uday brings a related insight into the Creator-and-game story, making identity and remembrance easier to visualize. Read their connection through the verses above: the game designed before entry is Uday’s explanation, while the cited passages develop awareness, oneness, and surrender.

“Untouched” describes the intended spiritual state, not an instruction to become emotionless. Laughing, crying, love, and anger can be experienced. There is no test requiring a feeling to disappear instantly. The movie and lotus help make remembrance understandable during everyday experience.

Within Uday’s teaching, natural care follows as this recognition becomes clear. It is the reason for returning to the root in every exercise. Understanding grows through enquiry, remembrance, and the way we meet actual people and situations. Return to the meaning rather than measuring yourself by one passing feeling.

The exercises invite you to examine what the teaching means in a particular scene: which role has absorbed you, what outcome you demand, and what remembering the shared Creator changes.
